title: Munich Court Holds Google Liable for False AI Overviews: What the Preliminary Injunction Means for Insurers' Chatbots
summary: On May 28, 2026 the Regional Court of Munich issued a temporary injunction treating Google's AI Overviews as Google's own content; Google said on June 11 it was reviewing the decision. Insurance Business draws lessons for insurers using generative AI.
description:
A German court has said that a technology company is responsible for what its artificial intelligence says, and insurance professionals are paying attention. On May 28, 2026, the Regional Court of Munich issued a temporary injunction against Google over its AI Overviews feature, according to an Insurance Business analysis headed "What the Munich Google ruling means for insurers." This article summarises that analysis. An earlier version of this article said that Google confirmed on June 12 that it would appeal. The report we reviewed says Google stated on June 11 that it is reviewing the decision, which is not yet final, and it does not describe a specific appeal, so the article now reflects that. The ruling is a preliminary measure and the case may develop further, so readers should check for current news.

What happened? The court issued a temporary injunction barring Google from repeating false statements about two Munich-based publishers. AI Overviews, Google's feature that shows AI-written summaries at the top of search results, had linked the publishers to scams and dubious business practices. Those claims appeared in none of the sources that the feature cited. In other words, the AI produced statements that its own references did not support.

How did the court reason? According to the report, the court treated AI Overviews as Google's own content and not a neutral pointer to third-party material, so Google bears direct liability. It drew a line between relaying content and authoring it. The AI rewrote and evaluated sources, in the words quoted in the report, in its own words and according to its own structure. The court also rejected the argument that links to sources allow users to verify the summaries, reasoning that citations do not transfer responsibility for the statement. It also noted that Google could have compared its output against the sources and did not.

What is the legal status? The report stresses that the ruling is a temporary injunction, not a final judgment. It does not bind US courts. The analysis argues that it previews a question that American courts may face, since Section 230 of US law protects hosting or transmitting others' content, not authoring it. The United States has no AI-specific liability statute, so existing defamation, negligence and consumer protection law would apply. Platforms may also redesign products to reduce exposure, which would reach users everywhere. Those are the analysts' arguments and not legal conclusions, and the report is not a prediction of how any court would rule.

Why does it matter for insurers? Insurers and brokers increasingly use generative tools to answer customer questions, summarise policies, assess eligibility and support claims decisions. The report says the risk is highest when such a tool makes checkable factual claims about named people or businesses and presents the output as a final answer. Examples it gives include policyholder coverage summaries, eligibility decisions, claims settlement recommendations and underwriting risk assessments. A chatbot that tells a customer they are covered when they are not, or that wrongly says a claim was fraudulent, could create legal and regulatory problems. The report quotes Forrester analyst Nikhil Lai as saying that AI outputs must be legally defensible, not just helpful.

What does the report recommend? It suggests three steps. First, make an inventory of every place where a generative system makes factual claims about third parties or customers, separating verbatim retrieval from synthesis. Second, ground customer-facing outputs in source material and keep logs that link sources to statements, so that a company can show where a statement came from. Third, review vendor contracts to clarify who bears liability when a third-party model produces false statements under the insurer's brand. These steps are a practical checklist and would be useful even if the Munich ruling were overturned.

What are the limits of the lesson? The case concerns a search engine and publishers, not insurers, and German law differs from the law elsewhere. The injunction is temporary. Insurers have regulatory duties, including fair treatment of customers, that exist whatever the court rules. Insurance regulators in Europe and the US are also developing guidance on AI use. A related development on this site is Marsh's report on AI exclusions, which shows that insurers are also deciding how to cover the risks that AI creates for their own customers.

What should customers know? People who use an insurer's chatbot should treat it as a guide and check important points, such as coverage and claims decisions, against the policy wording or a human adviser. Keeping a record of what a chatbot said can be helpful if a dispute arises.

The broader point is about responsibility. A company that deploys an AI tool under its own name is likely to be seen as speaking through that tool, whatever the technology behind it. Insurers already face rules on what they may say to customers, and generative AI makes it easier to say something wrong at scale, which is why controls, logging and human review matter.

This article summarises a published analysis and is not legal advice.
source_name: Insurance Business (analysis of the Munich Regional Court ruling)

key_points: On May 28, 2026 the Regional Court of Munich issued a temporary injunction barring Google from repeating false statements about two Munich-based publishers that its AI Overviews had linked to scams and dubious practices not found in the cited sources.

The court treated AI Overviews as Google's own content, not a neutral pointer to third-party material, because the AI rewrote and evaluated sources 'in its own words and according to its own structure'.
It rejected the argument that links let users verify the summaries, reasoning that citations do not transfer responsibility for the statement.
The ruling is a temporary injunction, not a final judgment, and does not bind US courts; Google said on June 11 that it is reviewing the decision.

The analysis says exposure is highest when a generative tool makes checkable factual claims about named people or businesses and presents the output as a final answer, such as coverage summaries, eligibility decisions or claims recommendations.
why_it_matters: Insurers are rolling out chatbots and AI assistants that explain coverage and claims. If a court treats AI output as the company's own statement, errors could create legal liability that a disclaimer may not remove.

title: NAIC Reviews Insurers' Data Centre Holdings and the Credit Ratings Behind Them as Private Bonds Reach 23.4% of Admitted Bonds
summary: According to Insurance Business citing the Financial Times, the NAIC is examining the ratings on data centre investments held by insurers; privately placed bonds were 23.4% of admitted bonds in 2025 per S&P Global Market Intelligence.
description:
Insurers have become major funders of the artificial intelligence building boom, and state insurance regulators want to know whether the credit ratings on that lending can be trusted. According to Insurance Business, which cites reporting by the Financial Times, the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) is reviewing insurers' data centre holdings and the credit ratings behind them. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article said the NAIC held the power to override ratings that differ from its own by more than three notches from January 1, 2026, without noting a later development. The Insurance Business report states that power has applied since that date, but KBRA's research release of June 8, 2026, says the amendment's original January 2026 implementation has been delayed. The two statements conflict, and we have not been able to resolve the difference, so readers should check the NAIC's current position.

What is the NAIC looking at? According to the report, the review covers tenant creditworthiness, lease exit clauses and construction firms' records on delays and cost overruns. These are the factors that determine whether a data centre will generate the cash flow needed to repay its lenders. A data centre leased to a strong technology company on a long lease is a different credit from a speculative building with a short lease or a tenant that can leave. The concern, the report says, is that ratings assigned during construction may not match the credit quality of finished, operating facilities.

Why does the rating matter? Ratings affect how much capital insurers must hold against a bond. A higher rating means a lower charge. If a rating were lowered after review, the insurer could face a higher capital charge on a large position. KBRA's research explains that such a charge would not itself be a loss on the bond, but it would reduce the insurer's capital ratio unless it raised more capital. That distinction is central to the debate about how closely regulators should scrutinise private ratings.

What is the discretion amendment? The report says that, from January 1, 2026, the NAIC can challenge and override credit ratings that differ from its own analysis by more than three notches. The power is described as covering public and private ratings. KBRA describes the amendment as adopted in August 2024, allowing the NAIC's Securities Valuation Office to review and challenge ratings it does not consider a reasonable measure of risk. The difference between the descriptions, including whether a three-notch threshold applies, is one that readers should check against NAIC documents.

How big is the private bond market for insurers? S&P Global Market Intelligence, cited in the report, says privately placed bonds made up 23.4% of insurers' admitted bonds in 2025, up from 18.3% in 2021. Moody's estimates that about 20% of US life insurers' fixed income portfolios are tied to private and illiquid bonds, a figure that other reporting on this site puts at $807 billion at the end of 2025. The two measures use different definitions, so the percentages are not directly comparable, but both show that private assets are a large and growing part of insurer balance sheets.

What are other authorities doing? The report says that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has met state insurance commissioners on the issue. In a statement in May, the Treasury called for fit-for-purpose regulation that balances innovation and risk. Moody's has said that regulators are paying more attention to transparency in portfolios. The NAIC's president, Scott White, has been quoted in other coverage as saying that transparency in life insurance portfolios is a top 2026 priority.

What does this mean for the AI boom? Data centres need very large amounts of capital, and long-term lenders such as life insurers are natural providers of it. The scrutiny does not mean that the loans are in trouble; the reports do not claim that any insurer has suffered a loss on a data centre investment. Rather, the question is whether the rating on a loan during construction reflects the risk of the finished asset, and whether the capital held against it is appropriate. If the review leads to tighter treatment, insurers might demand higher yields, shift to other assets or raise capital, with effects that would show up gradually.

The review also illustrates a wider shift. Insurers once held mostly public corporate and government bonds that anyone could price from market quotes. As they move into private loans, project finance and structured deals, regulators and ratings users depend more on the quality of the underlying credit analysis, which is harder for outsiders to check. That is why transparency and disclosure feature so heavily in current regulatory discussion.

For policyholders, the main point is that insurers' investments matter to their long-term security, and regulators are paying attention. Customers who want more detail can look at an insurer's financial strength ratings and its public disclosures about private and structured assets. This article reports published information, not a forecast, and is not investment advice.
source_name: Insurance Business (citing the Financial Times and S&P Global Market Intelligence)

key_points: The NAIC is reviewing insurers' data centre holdings and their credit ratings, including tenant creditworthiness, lease exit clauses and construction firms' records on delays and cost overruns.
The concern is that ratings assigned during construction may not match the credit quality of finished, operating facilities, which matters because ratings drive insurers' capital charges.

The NAIC's discretion amendment lets it challenge ratings that differ from its own analysis by more than three notches; the article says this has applied since January 1, 2026, although KBRA's June release says implementation was delayed.
Privately placed bonds made up 23.4% of insurers' admitted bonds in 2025, up from 18.3% in 2021, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence.
Moody's estimates about 20% of US life insurers' fixed income portfolios are tied to private and illiquid bonds; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has met state insurance commissioners on the issue.
why_it_matters: Insurers are among the biggest lenders to data centres and AI infrastructure. If the ratings on those loans prove too optimistic, insurers could need more capital, which would affect annuity pricing, the supply of infrastructure finance and policyholder confidence.

title: Specialty Insurance Rates Fall Back to 2020 Levels, WTW Survey Finds, as Property and Energy Lead the Softening
summary: WTW's Specialty Insurance Marketplace Survey, reported on May 6, 2026, says its rate index fell 10 points to 2020 levels, with 75% of 42 classes showing decreases at January 1 renewals, while general liability and medical malpractice moved counter-cyclically.
description:
Specialty insurance prices are falling faster than the industry expected. That is the central finding of WTW's Specialty Insurance Marketplace Survey, known as SIMS, reported by Insurance Journal on May 6, 2026. According to the report, rates fell during 2025 and at the January 1, 2026 renewals at a pace that outstripped forecasts by brokers and insurers alike. The survey's rate index dropped 10 points, taking pricing back to the levels last seen in 2020. This article summarises WTW's published findings. An earlier version also said that the January 2026 figures reflected benign catastrophe experience and abundant capacity across all classes; the report ties the benign catastrophe point specifically to property and energy, and that is how it is presented here.

What does the survey cover? WTW says SIMS reflects about $250 billion of gross written premium over a ten-year cycle, including $45 billion in 2025. It spans specialty insurers in London, Bermuda and the US excess and surplus lines (E&S) market. The data comes directly from clients of WTW Insurance Consulting and Technology and is not derived from broker estimates. The global specialty market leader at WTW, Richard Clarkson, is the named spokesperson in the report.

How large is the fall? The report says specialty rates rose about 45% cumulatively between 2017 and the market peak in 2023. Roughly half of that gain has been erased over the past two years. WTW adds that expected 2025 performance, once exposure trends are taken into account, has unwound gains back to 2021 levels. Rates alone are back at 2020 levels. A further sign of competition is that 2025 was the first year since 2018 in which rate adequacy for new business was lower than for renewal business. In practice, this means insurers were prepared to price new customers more aggressively than the customers they already had, a typical sign of insurers competing for share.

How widespread is the softening? According to the report, 75% of the 42 material classes that the survey tracks showed rate decreases at the January 2026 renewals, measured gross of claims trend. A year earlier, the figure was 30%. Aggregate rates fell 5% gross of claims trend and 8% net of claims trend. The net figure adjusts for actuarially estimated claims cost inflation that rate data alone do not capture. In plain terms, once the rising cost of claims is considered, the real price decline is larger than the headline rate change.

Where is it sharpest? Property and energy lines saw the steepest decreases, which WTW attributes to benign catastrophe experience and distorted frequency and severity trends. Marine, financial institutions and professional liability followed. Higher geopolitical tensions partly offset the decline, according to the report. The report does not give class-by-class percentage figures in the version summarised here, so readers who need figures for a particular line should consult the full WTW survey or their broker.

Which lines are going the other way? General liability and medical malpractice are moving counter-cyclically, meaning they are not following the market down. WTW cites substantial concerns about social inflation and nuclear jury verdicts, and also points to expanding litigation funding. Social inflation is the term used for claims costs rising faster than general inflation because of larger court awards and settlements. Nuclear verdicts are jury awards that are extremely large. WTW says it does not believe this trend is sustainable, but acknowledges uncertainty about short-term changes. That wording is important: the firm is describing a risk and a view, not a certain outcome.

What does this mean for buyers? Companies buying specialty cover, such as energy firms, shipowners, banks and professional-services businesses, are generally in a better negotiating position than they were at the peak. Lower rates mean lower costs of risk transfer, and buyers may be able to obtain broader terms or higher limits for the same spend. Buyers in general liability and medical malpractice may not see the same relief.

What does this mean for insurers? The cycle has turned, but the 2017 to 2023 increases mean many insurers entered the softening with strong margins. The question is how far prices fall before returns suffer. WTW's inclusion of claims-trend data is intended to give a fuller view of expected profitability than rate data alone, helping carriers test business plans and assess rate adequacy. The Insurance Journal summary of the report does not include a forecast for mid-year renewals. Investors and regulators will likely watch whether competition on price leads to looser underwriting.

For the wider economy, specialty insurance is the backstop for complex risks. Its pricing cycle affects the cost of building energy projects, moving cargo and running financial institutions. The 2020 level is a useful marker, but it is not a prediction: exposures, claims costs and legal conditions have all changed since then. This article summarises WTW's published survey and is not an investment recommendation or a forecast of future pricing.
source_name: WTW Specialty Insurance Marketplace Survey (via Insurance Journal)

key_points: WTW's SIMS rate index fell 10 points through 2025 and the January 1, 2026 renewals, returning to 2020 levels, faster than brokers and insurers had forecast.
Rates rose about 45% cumulatively from 2017 to the 2023 peak; roughly half of that gain has been erased in two years.
75% of 42 material classes showed rate decreases at January 2026 renewals (gross of claims trend), up from 30% in 2024; aggregate rates fell 5% gross and 8% net of claims trend.
Property and energy saw the steepest decreases, followed by marine, financial institutions and professional liability; general liability and medical malpractice moved counter-cyclically.
The survey covers about $250 billion of gross written premium over a ten-year cycle, including $45 billion in 2025, from London, Bermuda and US excess and surplus lines insurers.
why_it_matters: Specialty insurance covers hard-to-place risks such as energy, marine and professional liability. A fast softening gives buyers lower prices, but it also pressures insurers' margins at a time when WTW warns that litigation costs in liability lines keep rising.

title: Lemonade's Q1 2026: Revenue Up 71% to $258 Million, In-Force Premium $1.33 Billion, and a Tesla FSD Insurance Push
summary: Lemonade reported Q1 2026 revenue of $258 million (up 71%), in-force premium of $1.33 billion (up 32%) and a narrower net loss of $35.8 million, and expects its first positive adjusted EBITDA quarter in Q4 2026.
description:
Lemonade, the digital insurer that uses artificial intelligence in sales and claims, is growing quickly while its losses shrink, according to its first-quarter 2026 results. Reinsurance News reported on April 29, 2026, that revenue was $258 million, up 71% from a year earlier. The company attributes the rise to higher gross earned premium and better premium retention, from lower quota share cession rates that took effect in the third quarter of 2025. A quota share is an arrangement in which an insurer passes a fixed share of its premiums and claims to a reinsurer, so ceding less means keeping more of the revenue. This article summarises those results and Lemonade's autonomous car insurance launch. An earlier version of this article stated that the stock rose 10.45% on June 10 and fell 9.3% on June 4, and was down about 26% for the year. We could not verify those share-price figures in the sources reviewed, so they have been removed. Share prices change daily, and readers should check a current market source.

What do the Q1 numbers show? In-force premium, the annualised value of policies in effect, rose 32% to $1.33 billion. Customers rose 23% to 3,142,581. Earned premiums were $306.2 million, up 31%. Gross profit was $100.1 million, up 159%, and adjusted gross profit was $100.8 million, up 119%. The net loss narrowed to $35.8 million from $62.4 million in the first quarter of 2025. The adjusted EBITDA loss was $17.1 million, down from $47 million. Reinsurance News says the net loss ratio improved by 19 percentage points, which it credits to better underwriting and to the absence of the California wildfire impact that hit the first quarter of 2025. Lemonade said it continues to expect its first adjusted EBITDA-positive quarter in the fourth quarter of 2026. Adjusted EBITDA is a non-standard measure that excludes certain costs, so it is not the same as net profit, and the company still reports a net loss.

What is the autonomous car product? According to Crowdfund Insider, Lemonade announced Autonomous Car Insurance on January 21, 2026, targeting self-driving vehicles, starting with Tesla's Full Self-Driving (FSD) system. It builds on Lemonade's existing pay-per-mile model and adds tools to separate human-driven miles from autonomous miles, taking account of the specific software in use. The article reports a 50% reduction in per-mile premiums for miles driven with FSD engaged, but labels it as reported and traces it to a social media post, not an official Lemonade statement. It also says that development involved a partnership with Tesla that gave Lemonade access to vehicle telemetry, but cites no source for that claim, so readers should treat the Tesla data arrangement as unconfirmed. The article gives no base rates, and does not name the states where the product is available.

What did Lemonade say? Co-founder and president Shai Wininger is quoted as saying that legacy providers view a Tesla as just another automobile with a standard driver profile. The point is that, if a car drives itself some of the time, the risk is different from a conventional car with a human driver, and pricing could reflect that. Critics, the article says, question data privacy and the reliability of early autonomous systems. Lemonade says it emphasises openly disclosed, permission-based data handling and that customers control their own information. Whether autonomous driving reduces accident risk enough to justify big discounts is still an open question, and this article does not take a view.

Why is the stock volatile? The Crowdfund Insider article says Lemonade shares rose more than 15% on the news in January, reaching their highest level since mid-2021. Insurtech companies have attracted strong swings in sentiment, because investors are weighing rapid growth against a history of losses. Lemonade's results show growth and improving margins, but the company is not yet profitable on a net basis.

What are the risks? Growth could stall, claims could rise, particularly from weather events, and regulators may scrutinise AI-driven pricing. The reinsurance structure matters: retaining more premium raises revenue but also exposes the company to more of its own claims. In auto insurance, competition is intense, and the product depends on data and regulatory approval in each state.

What does it mean for customers? A customer who drives a Tesla with FSD might see lower per-mile rates if the product is available and the discount applies, but the details vary and the sources do not give a price. Customers who value privacy should read what data is collected. Everyone should compare quotes.

For readers new to insurtech, the key measures to follow are in-force premium, which shows the size of the book, the loss ratio, which shows whether pricing covers claims, and the path to positive adjusted EBITDA. Lemonade's guidance puts that milestone in the fourth quarter of 2026, which investors will test against the next quarterly reports.

This article reports company results and press coverage. It is not investment advice.

In-force premium rose 32% to $1.33 billion, customers rose 23% to 3,142,581 and earned premiums were $306.2 million, up 31%.
The net loss narrowed to $35.8 million from $62.4 million, and the adjusted EBITDA loss to $17.1 million from $47 million; Lemonade expects its first adjusted EBITDA-positive quarter in Q4 2026.

why_it_matters: Lemonade is one of the best-known AI-driven insurers. Its results show whether a digital model can grow quickly and approach profit, while its autonomous-car product tests whether driving-system data can change how car insurance is priced.

title: Indian Travellers Are Buying Travel Insurance in Bigger Numbers and With Larger Cover as Geopolitical Risk Reshapes Trips, Policybazaar Says
summary: Policybazaar data reported on May 9, 2026 shows travel insurance purchases up 22% year on year, with more travellers choosing $250,000 cover, 75% taking medical cover and solo travel above 76% of trips.
description:
More Indians are buying travel insurance, and they are buying bigger policies. That is the picture from data from Policybazaar, an Indian online insurance marketplace, reported by Outlook Money on May 9, 2026, with related coverage by Business Today. According to the report, travel insurance policy purchases rose by 22% compared with the previous year. This article summarises those reports. An earlier version of this article said that the number of travellers buying cover above $250,000 almost doubled, that 82% of Indian outbound travellers skip travel protection, that Japan bookings rose 17% and that UAE bookings fell more than 70%. We could not find those figures in the reports we reviewed, so they have been removed. The figures below are the ones the reports contain.

What is behind the growth? The report points to several factors. Overseas medical treatment and medical evacuation are expensive, and travellers are aware of the cost. It also names the US-Iran war as a recent source of Middle East tension, and says insurers are offering more flexible policies for cancellations and interruptions. Policybazaar's data does not by itself prove that geopolitical events caused the increase, and it may also reflect growth in overseas travel, rising incomes and more online purchasing. The report does not give an estimate of how much each factor contributes.

How much cover are people buying? Basic policies with about $10,000 of cover were once common, the report says. More travellers now choose plans with $250,000 of cover, because medical bills abroad, particularly in countries such as the United States, can be far higher than the older, smaller limits. The report does not give the proportion of travellers who buy the larger plans, so we cannot say how widespread the shift is.

What do people want covered? The report gives these figures: 75% of travellers opt for medical cover, making it the most important reason to buy travel insurance. Nearly 50% are considering trip cancellation cover, and 40% are considering evacuation cover. Evacuation cover pays for transport to a suitable hospital or home after a serious illness or injury, and costs for such transport can be very high. Solo travel makes up over 76% of trips, according to Manas Kapoor of Policybazaar. Travelling alone can increase the importance of insurance because there is no companion to help in an emergency, though the report does not draw that conclusion explicitly.

What does travel insurance typically not cover? This is general information and not drawn from the reports above, so readers should check their own policy. Many policies exclude losses caused by war or by events that were already known when the policy was bought, so buying cover after a conflict has started may not protect against disruption from that conflict. Pre-existing medical conditions, adventure activities and travel against government advice are other common exclusions or limitations. A cancellation benefit may cover only certain listed reasons. The only reliable way to know is to read the policy wording and ask the insurer or seller before buying.

How should a traveller choose? Compare the sum insured for medical expenses against the cost of care in the destination. Check whether evacuation is included and to what limit. Look at the cancellation and interruption terms and the exclusions for war, terrorism and civil unrest. Check the claims process, including whether the insurer has a cashless network for hospitals abroad. The price of a policy is usually small compared with the cost of a trip, but a cheap policy with low limits may not be useful in a serious emergency.

Is there a protection gap? Many travellers still travel without cover. The reports we reviewed do not provide a figure for how many, and we do not give one. The point stands that insurance is optional for most destinations, though some countries require proof of cover for visas.

What does it mean for insurers? Rising demand and larger cover raise premium volumes, but also expose insurers to higher claims if medical costs abroad keep rising or if conflicts disrupt travel at scale. Insurers adjusting their policies to be more flexible on cancellations may face higher claims in return. The Insurance Business reports on war-risk marine cover, covered elsewhere on this site, show how conflicts can quickly reprice risk in specialist markets.

A final practical point concerns timing. Cover that is bought soon after booking a trip often includes better protection for cancellation, because the reasons for cancelling have not yet arisen. Travellers should also keep records, including receipts, medical reports and airline notices, because insurers usually require documents for claims. Those who travel often may find an annual multi-trip policy cheaper than buying separate policies, though the limits and the maximum length of each trip should be checked first.

This article is general information based on press reports of marketplace data. It is not insurance advice, and Policybazaar's figures reflect its own customers and not the whole market.

Basic policies with about $10,000 cover were once common; more travellers now choose plans with $250,000 cover because of rising overseas treatment and evacuation costs.
Medical cover is chosen by 75% of travellers; nearly 50% are considering trip cancellation cover and 40% evacuation cover.

The article names the US-Iran war as a source of Middle East tension, and says insurers are offering more flexible policies for cancellations and interruptions.
why_it_matters: Medical costs abroad can be very high, and trips can be disrupted by conflict or flight cancellations. Understanding what travel insurance covers, and what it excludes, matters more as geopolitical risks rise.

title: National Roofing Week 2026: Why Insurers and Resilience Groups Say a Stronger Roof Is a Home's First Line of Defence
summary: During National Roofing Week (June 7-13, 2026, run by the NRCA), Triple-I, IBHS and the US SBA highlighted roof upgrades, IBHS's FORTIFIED standard and SBA disaster-loan increases of up to 20% for mitigation.
description:
A roof is the part of a building that takes the first hit from wind, hail and rain, and insurers and resilience groups say it deserves more attention. National Roofing Week 2026, which ran from June 7 to June 13, is organised by the National Roofing Contractors Association (NRCA), which says the week promotes public awareness of how essential roofs are, the positive contributions of the roofing industry, and the value of hiring a professional contractor. Within that week, the Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I) published a blog on June 8, 2026, by Loretta L. Worters titled "Partnering for Resilience: Protecting Homes Through Stronger Roofs," describing the shared view of Triple-I, the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety (IBHS) and the US Small Business Administration (SBA). This article summarises that blog and the NRCA information. An earlier version of this article said that Triple-I, IBHS and the SBA were running the week itself, and linked it to record severe-convective-storm losses. The week is run by the NRCA, and the blog does not give storm-loss statistics, so both points have been corrected.

What is the problem? The Triple-I blog says roof damage is a leading driver of insured losses and recovery costs. Water intrusion through a damaged roof can also destroy interiors, equipment, inventory and critical infrastructure, leading to business interruptions and financial hardship. For a household, that can mean displacement while repairs are made; for a small business, it can mean closing its doors. The blog does not give loss figures, and we do not supply any.

What do the experts recommend? According to the blog, stronger roofs can reduce damage, improve resilience and support long-term insurance affordability, and IBHS, Triple-I and the SBA are aligned on the idea that investing in resilience works. IBHS research links modest roof improvements to much lower storm damage and insurance losses. Examples include stronger deck attachments, sealed roof decks, impact-resistant materials, enhanced edge protection and better water barriers. These upgrades are most cost-effective when a roof is being replaced, because the work is already under way and the incremental cost is smaller than a separate project. A homeowner planning a re-roof can therefore ask the contractor which of these measures could be included.

What is FORTIFIED? IBHS's FORTIFIED programme is a voluntary construction and re-roofing standard that aims to close the gap between minimum building codes and true resilience. Codes set the minimum legal standard, which may not reflect the best available knowledge on storm protection. FORTIFIED goes further for roofs, and in some states insurers and governments recognise it through discounts or grants. The Triple-I blog does not list state programmes, and the availability and size of any discount vary by insurer and state, so homeowners should ask their insurers. Triple-I has also published separate material on state roof grant programmes.

What help is there for small businesses? The blog says small businesses are especially vulnerable and that upfront cost is a major barrier. It points to SBA financing, technical assistance and mitigation programmes. Specifically, SBA disaster loans can be increased by up to 20% for mitigation work, such as roof upgrades, and borrowers have up to two years from loan approval to request this funding. In other words, a business that borrows to repair damage after a disaster may be able to borrow somewhat more to rebuild in a stronger way. This is an existing programme, and the exact terms are set by the SBA, so businesses should check the current rules.

What other resources are listed? The blog lists Triple-I's Roof Toolkit, IBHS's Roofing Roadmaps, a National Roofing Week infographic, and a Triple-I article on how roofs affect home and business insurance. The page does not include details of insurer discounts.

Why does this matter for insurance? Roof age and condition are factors many insurers consider when deciding whether to offer cover and at what price. Some insurers have introduced special roof-related deductibles or limits on payments for older roofs, though the blog does not discuss these practices and they vary by company and state. A roof that is newer and built to a higher standard is likely to suffer less from storms, which benefits both the owner and the insurer. Whether this leads to a lower premium depends on the insurer and the location.

What can homeowners do? Inspect the roof regularly and after storms, keep records of repairs, and ask a licensed contractor about improvements when replacing it. Ask an insurer about the effect of roof age and materials on cover, and whether any discount applies for resilient roofs. Check local codes and permits. For small businesses, ask about SBA mitigation options before borrowing.

This article is general information drawn from published material by industry and trade groups, which have an interest in promoting roof investment. It is not a recommendation to buy any product or service.

title: Kemper Swings to a Q1 Loss as California Auto Pushes Specialty Combined Ratio to 106.7%; Stephen McAnena Named CEO
summary: Kemper reported a first-quarter 2026 net loss of $1.7 million as its Specialty P&C combined ratio rose to 106.7% from 92.7%, driven by California personal auto claims; Stephen McAnena became CEO on June 1.
description:
Kemper, a US insurer focused on specialty personal auto, started 2026 with a loss, and the company's own figures point to California as the main cause. In its first-quarter 2026 earnings release, filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, Kemper reported a net loss of $1.7 million, or $0.03 per diluted share. A year earlier it had net income of $99.7 million, or $1.54 per share. Adjusted consolidated net operating income, a measure that excludes certain items, was $12.5 million, or $0.21 per share, down from $106.4 million, or $1.65 per share. An earlier version of this article said that Kemper's shares were down 43.5% for the year, and that the company had sold its Newins agency business to Confie in April. We could not confirm either point in the company documents or in the other reports we reviewed, so they have been removed. The leadership details below come from Insurance Business.

What went wrong? The core of the story is in the Specialty Property and Casualty segment. Its adjusted net operating income fell to $0.1 million from $97.9 million. The combined ratio, which adds claims and expenses and divides the total by premiums earned, rose to 106.7% from 92.7%. A ratio above 100% means an insurer paid out more than it earned in premiums on that business. Within personal auto, the underlying loss and loss adjustment expense ratio reached 87.7%, up from 70.1%. Kemper attributes the increase mainly to claim severity and frequency in California, lower volumes, and a $28.0 million Florida statutory profit limit refund. In plain terms, claims in California were both more frequent and more expensive, and the company has fewer premiums to spread them across.

How did other parts of the business do? Commercial auto grew its policies in force by 10% compared with a year earlier, with an underlying combined ratio of 92.4%. Life insurance, a smaller segment, increased adjusted net operating income to $18.0 million from $17.2 million. Total revenues fell by $85.8 million to $1,107.2 million. Kemper Corporation shareholders' equity was $2,649.6 million. Book value per share was $45.05 and adjusted book value per share was $27.79. The quarterly dividend was $0.32 per share. These figures show a company that remains profitable in some areas and well capitalised, but whose largest segment is under pressure.

What is the company doing about it? Kemper says it has identified $60 million in run-rate savings from restructuring, and it has already put $50 million of those actions in place. The interim chief executive, C. Thomas Evans, Jr., said in the release: "Our results this quarter reflect continued pressure in parts of the business, particularly California personal auto."

There has also been a change at the top. Insurance Business reports that Kemper announced on May 27, 2026, that Stephen J. McAnena would become president and chief executive and join the board effective June 1, 2026. He comes from Horace Mann, where he was executive vice president and chief operating officer, and has more than 30 years of insurance experience across property and casualty, group benefits, life and annuity lines. He succeeds Joseph P. Lacher, Jr., who led Kemper for nearly a decade and left abruptly in October 2025, when the board decided on October 14 that he would step down immediately. Evans, a Kemper veteran since 1992, served as interim CEO and returns to his role as executive vice president, secretary and general counsel. The report describes McAnena's mandate as centred on execution: tightening underwriting discipline, completing the restructuring and rebuilding investor confidence. That description is the report's characterisation, and Kemper has not published a detailed plan in the materials we reviewed.

Why does California matter so much? California is the largest state auto market in the United States, and it has been difficult for insurers because of rising repair costs, more expensive vehicles and parts, and the state's rate-approval system, which can delay price increases. Kemper's release refers to claim severity and frequency, which is consistent with those pressures, but the filing does not give a detailed breakdown of causes. Readers should therefore be careful not to attribute the loss to any one factor beyond what the company states.

What does it mean for customers? When an insurer's auto results deteriorate, customers can see changes at renewal: higher premiums, stricter eligibility or fewer new policies. Kemper has said that volumes were lower in the quarter, which suggests that it has already been managing its book. Policyholders who see large increases can compare quotes from several insurers, since conditions differ by company and region. For Kemper's shareholders and analysts, the question is how quickly price increases and underwriting actions bring the combined ratio back below 100%.

This article summarises Kemper's published results and a trade press report on its management change. It is not investment advice.

The Specialty P&C combined ratio rose to 106.7% from 92.7%, meaning claims and expenses exceeded premiums earned.
Personal auto's underlying loss and LAE ratio reached 87.7% from 70.1%, mainly on California claim severity and frequency, lower volumes and a $28.0 million Florida statutory profit limit refund.
Commercial auto grew policies in force 10% with an underlying combined ratio of 92.4%; life insurance operating income rose to $18.0 million.
Stephen McAnena, formerly of Horace Mann, became president and CEO on June 1, 2026; Kemper has identified $60 million in run-rate savings and actioned $50 million.
why_it_matters: Kemper shows how quickly personal auto profits can reverse when claim costs rise faster than prices. For drivers, it is a reminder that insurers under pressure may raise rates, tighten underwriting or reduce policies in problem states.

title: Australia's Superannuation Assets Slip 1% in the March Quarter to A$4.44 Trillion but Remain Up 7.9% on the Year, APRA Data Shows
summary: APRA's March 2026 quarterly statistics, released May 28, show total superannuation assets of A$4,437.9 billion, down 1.0% on the quarter and up 7.9% on the year, with contributions up 11.3% and benefit payments up 12.3%.
description:
Australia's retirement savings system dipped slightly in the first quarter of 2026 but remains well ahead of a year ago. The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) released its quarterly superannuation statistics for the March 2026 quarter on May 28, 2026. Total superannuation assets were A$4,437.9 billion at March 31, 2026, which is about A$4.4 trillion. That is a fall of 1.0% over the quarter, but up 7.9% from A$4,111.4 billion a year earlier. This article summarises APRA's release. An earlier version cited secondary sources and said that nine mega funds each hold more than A$100 billion, and attributed the fall to the war in the Middle East. The APRA release itself does not make either statement, so they have been removed; the release gives the numbers but not the cause of the movement, and readers should not assume market conditions explain it without a source.

What do the headline numbers show? Over the year to March 2026, total assets rose by about A$326 billion. Over the March quarter alone they fell by 1.0%. APRA-regulated assets, which are held by the funds it supervises, were A$3,141.1 billion, up 8.7% from a year earlier. APRA's page describes this as about A$3.1 trillion. Other categories, with their year-on-year changes, were as follows. Self-managed super funds held A$1,057.6 billion, up 7.0% from A$988.0 billion. Exempt public sector superannuation schemes held A$178.4 billion, up 2.9% from A$173.4 billion. Life office statutory fund balances were A$60.8 billion, up 2.5% from A$59.3 billion. These categories are separate pieces of the same overall total, and together they explain why the total is larger than the APRA-regulated amount alone.

How much is going in? Total contributions for the year to March 2026 were A$226.1 billion, up 11.3%. Employer contributions were A$159.8 billion, up 8.4%, and member contributions were A$66.3 billion, up 19.1%. Employer contributions in Australia are largely compulsory, tied to the Superannuation Guarantee, so their growth reflects wages and the contribution rate. Member contributions are voluntary or additional, and a 19.1% rise is a large increase, although the APRA release does not give reasons. Possible explanations would be speculation on our part, and we do not offer one.

How much is coming out? Benefit payments for the year were A$143.5 billion, up 12.3%. Lump sum payments were A$79.7 billion, up 13.6%, and pension payments were A$63.8 billion, up 10.7%. Rising pension payments are consistent with a growing number of retirees drawing on their savings, which is a normal feature of a maturing system. The release does not break down payments by age or fund type.

What are the net flows? For entities with more than six members, APRA reports contributions of A$226.1 billion, up 11.3% from A$203.0 billion, and benefit payments of A$143.5 billion, up 12.3% from A$127.8 billion. Net contribution flows, defined as contributions plus net benefit transfers less benefit payments, were A$74.5 billion, up 9.6% from A$68.0 billion. In other words, more money continues to enter the system than leaves it, although benefit payments are growing slightly faster than contributions. The release does not include investment returns or member numbers, so it cannot show how much of the change in assets came from market performance.

Why does the quarterly fall matter? A 1.0% drop in a pool of this size equals tens of billions of Australian dollars, but it is small in comparison with the 7.9% annual gain. Short-term movements in super balances depend on financial markets, and members with long horizons usually experience such dips as part of normal volatility. Those closer to retirement are more exposed to the timing of market falls, which is why many funds offer lifecycle or default options that reduce risk with age. The APRA statistics are about the whole system and cannot say how any individual fund or member fared.

What should members do with this information? Aggregate data is a useful backdrop but not a guide to personal decisions. Members can check their own fund's returns, fees and investment option on its website or the government's comparison tools. They can also check that their employer is paying contributions on time. This article is general information based on a regulator's statistical release and is not financial advice.

It is also worth remembering what the figures leave out. They are totals in nominal Australian dollars, with no adjustment for inflation, and they cover assets in the accumulation and pension phases together. A rising total can reflect new contributions as much as investment gains, so the number alone says little about how well members are doing. The year-on-year rise of 7.9% is the net result of contributions, benefit payments and market movements combined.

For readers outside Australia, the figures show how large compulsory retirement saving can become. At A$4.4 trillion, super assets are significant for local markets, including property, infrastructure and equities. Regulators and policymakers watch these flows closely, because the system affects both retirement incomes and the economy. Data are subject to revision in later releases, and APRA publishes updated statistics each quarter.
source_name: Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA), Quarterly Superannuation Statistics, March 2026

APRA-regulated assets were A$3,141.1 billion (up 8.7%); self-managed super funds held A$1,057.6 billion (up 7.0%).
Contributions for the year to March 2026 were A$226.1 billion, up 11.3%, with member contributions up 19.1% to A$66.3 billion.

why_it_matters: Superannuation is the retirement savings of most Australian workers and one of the largest pools of investment capital in the world. A quarterly dip shows market risk, while rising contributions and payouts show a system that is both growing and maturing.

title: Alpen Capital: GCC Insurance Premiums Forecast to Reach $61.8 Billion by 2030, With Saudi Arabia the Fastest Grower
summary: Alpen Capital's GCC Insurance Industry report, covered by Khaleej Times on May 21, 2026, forecasts premiums of $61.8 billion by 2030 at a 4.9% CAGR, with Saudi Arabia growing at 5.9% and the UAE at 4.1%.
description:
Insurance in the Gulf is forecast to keep growing, but at a measured pace, according to Alpen Capital. The investment bank's GCC Insurance Industry report, covered by Khaleej Times on May 21, 2026, projects that gross written premiums in the six Gulf Cooperation Council countries will reach $61.8 billion by 2030, growing at a compound annual rate of 4.9% from 2025. Non-life insurance is projected to grow at 5.2% a year and to account for nearly 88% of regional premiums by 2030. This article summarises that coverage. An earlier version of this article gave the UAE forecast as $25.1 billion by 2030 and said the IMF expected about 5% UAE growth in 2026. The Khaleej Times article we reviewed gives UAE health and property and casualty figures but not a 2030 UAE total, and does not mention the IMF forecast, so those two points have been removed.

Which countries lead? The forecasts by country are compound annual growth rates for 2025 to 2030. Saudi Arabia is expected to grow at 5.9%, which makes it the largest and fastest-growing market in the region. Kuwait is forecast at 5.5% and the UAE at 4.1%, although the article notes that some industry estimates suggest near-term growth in the UAE could be higher. Alpen Capital's chief executive, TM Lakshmanan, said that the expansion of mandatory insurance lines is a key support for growth. Mandatory lines, such as compulsory health or motor cover, create a base of demand that does not depend on the economic cycle.

What is happening in the UAE? The article says the UAE market could grow by 10% to 15% in 2026 after a sharp rise in premiums in late 2025. It values health insurance at about $10.1 billion and property and casualty at about $20.1 billion. The expatriate population is described as a major structural driver, especially for employer-backed health and group schemes. Non-oil economic growth, tourism, aviation, logistics, real estate and infrastructure are also deepening insurance penetration. It is worth noting that the 10% to 15% estimate and the 4.1% five-year forecast refer to different periods and sources, so they should not be read as contradictory: one is a near-term view and the other is a long-run average.

Which products are growing? Cyber insurance is among the fastest-growing segments across the GCC. Demand is also rising for war-risk, marine, political-risk and cyber cover, particularly among shipping, logistics and airline companies and businesses exposed to supply-chain disruption. This fits the wider regional context. As covered elsewhere on this site, war-risk premiums for ships using the Strait of Hormuz have been very high during the Iran conflict, and insurers are working with government-backed facilities to provide cover.

What are the risks? The article lists geopolitical tensions, volatile oil prices, rising claims costs, climate-related events and operational risks. Rising reinsurance costs, high operating expenses, weaker investment returns and higher claims ratios are pressuring margins, especially for smaller insurers. Competition has also pushed some rates down: the article says some professional indemnity and cyber rates have eased by 5% to 20% this year. That is in line with the global softening seen in surveys from WTW and Lloyd's.

How is regulation changing the market? Regulators, including the Central Bank of the UAE, are tightening solvency and governance rules. The article says this is prompting portfolio cuts, balance-sheet strengthening and fresh capital raises. Mergers and acquisitions are expected to accelerate as insurers seek scale. Insurance penetration across the GCC remains below global averages, which points to long-term growth potential. Penetration means premiums as a share of economic output, so a low figure suggests that people and businesses buy less insurance relative to the size of the economy than in many other regions.

What does it mean for residents and businesses? For residents, growth in mandatory health and motor cover means that insurance is becoming a larger household cost, but competition in some commercial lines may lower costs for businesses. For companies, particularly in shipping, aviation and logistics, specialty cover is more available but also more complex to price. For investors, smaller insurers with weaker capital may be targets for consolidation. These are observations drawn from the report's themes, and Alpen Capital does not make company-specific recommendations in the coverage we reviewed.

One further point is that the GCC is not a single market. Saudi Arabia's growth is shaped by its large population and mandatory health cover, Kuwait's by a smaller base, and the UAE's by a large expatriate workforce and its role as a regional hub for reinsurers and brokers. Comparing the growth rates across countries therefore says as much about starting points as about future performance.

Forecasts of this kind rest on assumptions about economic growth, oil prices, population and regulation, and they can change quickly in a region exposed to conflict. Readers should treat the 2030 figure as a projection from one analyst, not as a certainty. This article reports Alpen Capital's analysis as covered by Khaleej Times and is not investment advice.
source_name: Alpen Capital GCC Insurance Industry report (via Khaleej Times)

key_points: Alpen Capital forecasts GCC gross written premiums of $61.8 billion by 2030, a 4.9% CAGR from 2025; non-life is projected to grow 5.2% a year and make up nearly 88% of premiums.
By country, Saudi Arabia is expected to grow 5.9% a year (the largest and fastest-growing market), Kuwait 5.5% and the UAE 4.1%, though some industry estimates see higher near-term UAE growth.
The UAE market could expand 10-15% in 2026 after a sharp rise in premiums in late 2025; health insurance is valued at about $10.1 billion and property and casualty at about $20.1 billion.
Cyber is among the fastest-growing segments, and demand for war-risk, marine and political risk cover is rising among shipping, logistics and airline businesses.
Some professional indemnity and cyber rates have eased 5-20% this year, while regulators tighten solvency and governance rules and consolidation is expected.
why_it_matters: The Gulf is one of the faster-growing insurance regions, driven by expatriate health cover, mandatory lines and large infrastructure projects. Its growth, price softening and tighter regulation will shape what companies and residents pay for cover and which insurers survive.

title: Lockton Reports $4.5 Billion in Fiscal 2026 Revenue, Up 12%, With US Revenue Near $3 Billion and Client Retention at 94%
summary: Lockton, the world's largest privately held independent insurance broker, reported fiscal 2026 revenue of about $4.5 billion, up 12% with 11% organic growth, its sixth straight year of double-digit organic growth.
description:
Lockton, the largest privately held independent insurance broker in the world, has reported another year of double-digit growth. According to the company's announcement for its fiscal year 2026, which ended on April 30, 2026, global revenue rose 12% to approximately $4.5 billion. Organic growth, which strips out the effect of acquisitions, was 11%. Lockton says this was its sixth consecutive year of double-digit organic growth. This article summarises the company's own announcement and the context it gives. Lockton is private, so these figures are self-reported and have not been audited by an outside party in anything we reviewed. An earlier version of this article described Lockton Re's new reinsurance licence in Saudi Arabia and launch in Dubai. Those details did not appear in the company announcement we reviewed, so they have been removed; the announcement refers instead to expansion in Saudi Arabia, Switzerland and Italy.

How did the regions perform? In the United States, revenue was just under $3 billion, up 11%, which Lockton says is the eighth straight year of double-digit growth in its US business. Client revenue retention was 94%, meaning the firm kept 94% of the revenue it had from existing clients. Lockton also says its People Solutions business, which covers employee benefits and related advice, passed $1 billion in revenue for the first time. Internationally, revenue grew about 15%, and People Solutions grew 27% outside the US. The firm expanded operations in Switzerland, Saudi Arabia and Italy. Lockton Re, the reinsurance broking arm, also grew about 15%, and it is investing in capital markets, cyber and credit offerings.

What does the firm say about technology? Lockton says that its AI-enabled platform, Lockton SAGE, will begin broader deployment in fiscal 2027. Ron Lockton, the chief executive, is quoted in the announcement as saying, "We see AI as an accelerator of human expertise, not a substitute for it." That wording is consistent with how most large brokers describe their approach: automation for routine work, with human advisers for judgement and negotiation. The announcement does not give details of how SAGE works or how many clients use it, so claims about its impact should be treated as the firm's expectation, not a measured result.

What is the market context? Lockton says that global property rates softened as capacity and competition increased, and that US casualty lines faced pricing pressure and elevated loss costs. That matches independent reports. WTW's survey, covered separately on this site, found that specialty rates have fallen back to 2020 levels, with property and energy leading, while general liability and medical malpractice moved the other way. For a broker, falling rates cut commission income per policy, since commissions are often a percentage of premium. Growth in a softening market therefore depends on winning new clients, selling more services and adding advisory and benefits work, and not on price increases alone. The People Solutions figures suggest that benefits advice is carrying some of that load.

Why does a broker's growth matter to readers outside the industry? Businesses buy insurance largely through brokers, so brokers influence which insurers a company approaches and how risks are described. Lockton's growth means it handles an increasing share of that flow, as it competes with the larger public brokers. Being privately held, it does not publish the full financial statements that listed brokers do, so the announcement gives limited information on profit margins, debt or acquisitions. Readers who want to compare Lockton with public brokers should be careful: organic growth is defined by each company, and private-company figures cannot be directly compared with filings.

There are some risks to watch. A prolonged softening could reduce commission income across the sector. Competition for talent is intense, and the firm's roughly 15,000 Associates are its main asset. Regulatory scrutiny of broker compensation and conflicts of interest has grown in several markets. Lockton's announcement does not discuss these issues, and this article does not suggest any specific problem at the firm. It simply notes what any reader should keep in mind when reading a company's own results.

For policyholders, the practical takeaway is that a broker's role extends beyond placing a policy. Large clients use brokers for claims advocacy, risk consulting, captives, and employee benefits strategy. Smaller businesses may find that buying through a broker or agent gives them access to markets they could not approach alone. When prices are falling, it is a good time to ask a broker to review limits, deductibles and terms, since buyers have more negotiating power than they did at the peak of the cycle.

In summary, Lockton's fiscal 2026 results show continued double-digit growth in a year when property pricing was softening. The numbers come from the firm itself, and the story they tell is of expansion in benefits, reinsurance broking and international markets. This article reports the company's announcement and is not investment advice.

US revenue was just under $3 billion, up 11%, the eighth straight year of double-digit growth; client revenue retention was 94% and People Solutions passed $1 billion for the first time.
International revenue grew about 15%, with People Solutions up 27%; the firm expanded in Switzerland, Saudi Arabia and Italy.
Lockton Re also grew about 15%, investing in capital markets, cyber and credit offerings.
Nearly 15,000 Associates work at the firm, and its AI-enabled platform Lockton SAGE begins broader deployment in fiscal 2027.
why_it_matters: Brokers sit between businesses and insurers, so their results show how commercial insurance demand and pricing are moving. Lockton's steady growth while property rates soften shows that advice, claims and benefits work can keep a broker growing even when premiums fall.

title: Canadian Insurers Urge Homeowners to Fortify Properties and Ask Ottawa to Keep Climate Risk a Priority as Wildfire Season Starts
summary: Bloomberg reported on April 14, 2026 that Canadian insurers are pressing homeowners to fireproof and floodproof their homes and urging Ottawa to update building codes, as premiums rose about 6% last year and 2024 claims hit a record C$9.4 billion.
description:
Canadian insurers are asking both homeowners and the federal government to do more about climate risk as the 2026 wildfire season begins. A Bloomberg report published by BNN Bloomberg on April 14, 2026, describes how the industry is encouraging owners to strengthen their homes and pressing Ottawa to keep climate on its agenda. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article named Intact Financial, TD Insurance and Wawanesa as taking part. The Bloomberg report we reviewed quotes only the chief executive of Definity, so the other names have been removed to avoid attributing statements to companies we could not confirm.

What are insurers asking homeowners to do? According to the report, insurers are encouraging owners to flood-proof and fire-proof their homes. Discounts are available for completing risk assessments or installing fire-resistant roofing and siding. This is part of a wider shift toward rewarding mitigation, which is also described in a CBC report on property-level wildfire assessment covered elsewhere on this site. For homeowners, the practical message is that investment in the home itself, such as fire-resistant materials, may reduce the risk and in some cases the premium. The report does not say how large the discounts are.

What are insurers asking governments to do? The industry wants building codes updated so that new homes can withstand climate risks. It wants investment in natural infrastructure, such as wetlands and green spaces that absorb floodwater. It also wants a halt to new construction in areas that are already prone to floods and wildfires. These are asks that affect planning and housing policy as well as insurance, and governments must weigh them against other priorities, including housing supply.

Why are insurers concerned? The report gives several figures. Home insurance premiums rose about 6% last year. Insurance claims hit a record C$9.4 billion in 2024, following the Jasper wildfire, a hailstorm in Calgary and flooding in Toronto. About 32 million hectares have burned in wildfires over the past three years. The federal government plans 3.9 million new homes, and according to the Insurance Bureau of Canada, roughly 500,000 of them could be in high-risk flood zones and over 200,000 in high-risk wildfire zones. The federal government says it has invested more than C$6.6 billion since 2015 in community preparedness and wildland fire management.

What is the political concern? The report says insurers fear that climate has slipped down the agenda as Prime Minister Mark Carney prioritises energy and trade. The chief executive of Definity is quoted as saying, "We're going to... keep it at the top of the table." The wording in the report is ellipsed, and we reproduce only the short phrase in the report. The tension is between building quickly and building safely: faster approvals and more homes can conflict with limits on construction in risky areas. The report presents the insurers' view, and the government's own response is limited to the funding figure above.

Is the industry in trouble? The report says insurers remain profitable. Net income rose 56.7% in 2025 and claims were lower than in 2024. It also notes that calamity-prone areas in Canada are still insurable, unlike in some other countries where insurers have withdrawn from high-risk regions. That is an important point. The concern is not that insurers are failing, but that they want to keep markets functioning in the face of rising risks. Strong profits can be read two ways: they show that the industry can absorb losses now, but they also show that premium increases have been significant, and a profitable industry makes a more credible advocate for long-term prevention.

What does it mean for homeowners? Premiums are likely to depend more on the characteristics of individual properties and areas. Homeowners in high-risk areas may face higher premiums or higher deductibles, and those who invest in mitigation may be rewarded. Prospective buyers can ask insurers about coverage and cost before purchasing a home, especially in flood or wildfire zones. The report does not give a forecast for premiums in 2026 and we do not offer one.

What should readers watch? Three things stand out: whether building codes are updated and applied, whether the federal and provincial governments limit construction in high-risk zones, and how the 2026 wildfire and flood season unfolds. A severe season would test the industry and the political attention given to mitigation. A mild one could make the issue less urgent, even though the long-term trend in risk is upward.

It is also worth noting what the report does not say. It does not give the size of the premium discounts, it does not set out which insurers are offering them, and it does not report any statement from the federal government beyond the funding figure. The picture is therefore the industry's own account of its concerns, delivered at the start of a season in which those concerns could be tested.

This article summarises a news report and is general information, not insurance or investment advice.

They are asking governments to update building codes, invest in natural infrastructure and stop new construction in areas already prone to floods and wildfires.
Home insurance premiums rose about 6% last year; claims hit a record C$9.4 billion in 2024 after the Jasper fire, a Calgary hailstorm and Toronto floods.
The Insurance Bureau of Canada says Ottawa's plan for 3.9 million new homes could put roughly 500,000 in high-risk flood zones and over 200,000 in high-risk wildfire zones.
The industry remains profitable, with net income up 56.7% in 2025 and lower claims than in 2024, and calamity-prone areas are still insurable.
why_it_matters: Canada is one of the countries where insurers still cover homes in disaster-prone areas. How the government, builders and homeowners respond to climate risk will determine whether that stays true and what premiums look like.

title: Lloyd's 2025: £10.6 Billion Profit, 87.6% Combined Ratio and a Softer Cycle Ahead as Seven New Syndicates Join and 13 More Follow
summary: Lloyd's reported 2025 pre-tax profit of £10.6 billion and an 87.6% combined ratio, while warning that capital inflows could pressure reinsurance pricing; Fitch says the market is well placed for a softer cycle.
description:
Lloyd's of London enters a softer pricing cycle from a position of strength, according to its own results and the credit rating agency Fitch. The market reported a pre-tax profit of £10.6 billion for 2025, up 10.1%, and gross written premium of £57.9 billion, up 4.2%. The combined ratio was 87.6%, compared with 86.9% in 2024, so the market remained solidly profitable on its underwriting. These figures were reported by Insurance Business on March 19, 2026. This article combines that report, an Insurance Business piece on competition in reinsurance, and Reinsurance News's coverage of Fitch's view. An earlier version of this article said Fitch had commented on reinsurance competition and capital inflows. In the reports we reviewed, Fitch's comments concern the soft cycle and Lloyd's financial strength, while the figures on new syndicates and enquiries come from Lloyd's itself. The article now reflects that.

What do the profit figures consist of? Underwriting profit was roughly stable at £5.2 billion, compared with £5.3 billion in 2024. Investment returns rose to £6.0 billion from £4.9 billion. The underlying combined ratio was 81.8%, up from 79.1%. The major claims ratio fell to 5.8% from 7.8%, while the attritional loss ratio, which covers routine claims, stayed at 47.9%. The expense ratio was 35.6%, up on higher commissions, business mix and currency effects. Prior-year reserve releases added 1.7 percentage points to the result. Premium growth came from volume up 10.3%, offset by a 3.7% fall in pricing and a 2.4% currency headwind. Total capital, reserves and subordinated debt rose 5.7% to £49.8 billion.

How strong is the capital? The central solvency ratio rose to 496% from 435%, while the market-wide solvency ratio was 200%, compared with 205% in 2024. Fitch adds that the reserve margin increased to £6.6 billion, within total net claims of £58.8 billion. Fitch says Lloyd's disciplined approach to underwriting, reserving and investment management leaves it well placed to navigate a softer pricing cycle over the next two years, and it expects Lloyd's credit profile to remain robust through 2026.

What is the competitive pressure? Lloyd's said in its report on reinsurance competition that rising competition could pressure reinsurance pricing in 2026 if capital keeps returning to the sector, particularly in the absence of significant catastrophe activity. The marketplace received more than 50 serious enquiries from prospective participants during the year. Seven new syndicates began operating in 2025, and 13 more launched on January 1, 2026. Reinsurance showed the strongest expansion of any line. Existing syndicates grew volume by 7.2% while new syndicates added 3.1%. Lloyd's also noted rising demand for political risk, credit and war-related cover, linked to the Russia-Ukraine war and tensions in the Middle East, as well as rising capital requirements and pressure on casualty reserves.

What does Fitch say about pricing and the Iran conflict? Fitch says risk-adjusted pricing fell 3.7% in 2025, reversing several years of increases, and it expects a steeper decline in 2026. On the Iran conflict, Fitch says Lloyd's has exposure through specialty lines such as marine and aviation war, political violence, trade credit and energy. It does not expect widespread claims from standard property or cyber policies and sees the effect mainly on earnings, though it warns that a prolonged conflict could increase volatility.

What is Lloyd's doing strategically? The March report says Lloyd's has set a five-year strategy aimed at sharper underwriting, greater efficiency and better use of its capital strength. Planned measures include modernising back-office operations and doubling the early-careers intake. Lloyd's chief executive Patrick Tiernan said the results give a firm foundation for the challenges and risks ahead. Sheila Cameron of the Lloyd's Market Association stressed the importance of keeping the combined operating ratio below 95% through the cycle, and Caroline Wagstaff of the London Market Group called the strategy a clear road map. Lloyd's itself expects pricing to become more challenging and volatility to rise, but says its strategic priorities are unchanged.

What does this mean for buyers and investors? For buyers of specialty and reinsurance cover, more capacity generally means lower prices and more flexible terms. For capital providers, the challenge is that new money can push prices below levels that give adequate returns. A market with a combined ratio in the high 80s has room to absorb price cuts, but that room is not unlimited, especially if catastrophe losses return. The experience of past cycles is that discipline can slip quickly when capacity is plentiful.

For readers new to the market, Lloyd's is not a single insurer but a marketplace in which syndicates, backed by capital providers, underwrite risks through brokers. That structure means new capital can enter quickly, as the 20 new syndicates in 2025 and 2026 show, and can also leave quickly if returns disappoint. It is why Lloyd's leaders talk so often about discipline: the market's reputation, and the central fund that supports it, depends on every syndicate pricing risk responsibly.

This article summarises published reports and company statements and is not investment advice.
