Risk-adjusted pricing fell 3.7% in 2025; Fitch expects a steeper decline in 2026 but says Lloyd's is well placed to navigate a softer pricing cycle over the next two years.
Seven new syndicates started in 2025 and 13 more on January 1, 2026; Lloyd's received more than 50 serious underwriting enquiries, with reinsurance showing the strongest expansion.
The central solvency ratio rose to 496% from 435% and the market-wide ratio was 200%; the reserve margin rose to £6.6 billion.
Fitch sees Iran-related exposure mainly in specialty lines such as marine and aviation war, political violence, trade credit and energy.
why_it_matters: Lloyd's is a bellwether for specialty and reinsurance pricing worldwide. Its message that capital is flowing in while rates slip suggests buyers will keep the advantage, and that underwriting discipline will decide which insurers keep earning profits.

title: Fitch: Japanese and Korean Insurers Are Set to Keep Buying Abroad, With About ¥4.5 Trillion Already Spent and 86% of It in the US
summary: A Fitch Ratings viewpoint of April 29, 2026 says Japanese insurers' major deals total about ¥4.5 trillion (US$35 billion), 86% in the US, and that Korean cross-border M&A reached about $2.6 billion in 2025, with concentration and capital risks to watch.
description:
Insurers in Japan and South Korea are going abroad for growth, and the credit rating agency Fitch expects the shopping to continue. In a viewpoint published by Insurance Journal on April 29, 2026, written by Fitch analysts Teruki Morinaga and Sue Kim, the agency says Japanese and Korean insurers have sharply increased overseas mergers and acquisitions and strategic investments in recent years, in both developed and emerging markets. This article summarises that commentary. An earlier version of this article listed a Mitsui Sumitomo stake in W.R. Berkley and described the Berkshire Hathaway and Tokio Marine partnership as raising Tokio Marine's M&A capacity. Neither point appears in the Fitch text, so they have been removed; the Berkshire partnership is covered in a separate article.

Why are they buying abroad? Fitch points to demographics and slow growth at home. In Japan, the population has declined for 14 consecutive years, which weighs on domestic growth, and Fitch expects Japanese life insurers' underwriting profit margins to peak within five to ten years because of demographic pressure. In Korea, premium growth is slowing because of an ageing population, low economic growth, interest rate cuts and stricter K-ICS capital rules. Fitch projects Korean insurance revenue growth below 5% in 2026. For insurers with large capital bases, buying growth abroad is a response.

The pattern in Japan is established. Fitch says more than half of the Japanese insurers it rates have done M&A in the past decade. Major deals total about ¥4.5 trillion, or about US$35 billion, and 86% of that is in the United States. The agency notes that the US is the only major developed market larger than Japan with steady population growth, and that North America accounts for roughly 40% of global non-life premiums. It lists advantages of the US for Japanese buyers: a familiar business language, transparent corporate law, strong regulation, and the ability to take 100% ownership. It also says Japanese insurers are cash-ready and can outbid private equity buyers. Not every overseas move has worked: Fitch cites Meiji Yasuda's 2023 sale of its stake in PT Avrist Assurance in Indonesia and Dai-ichi's May 2025 plan to divest its stake in Ocean Life Insurance in Thailand as examples of failed Asian deals.

The key deals are named. Tokio Marine entered the US in the early 2000s and has acquired three US insurers. Dai-ichi Life also entered in the early 2000s and acquired Protective Life. Sompo acquired Aspen Insurance Holdings in 2025. Nippon Life announced two acquisitions in 2024, including Resolution Life Group for ¥1.2 trillion, or US$8.4 billion, and is the last major Japanese life insurer to enter North America. Fitch's insurer financial strength ratings for the Japanese groups include AA-/Stable for Tokio Marine & Nichido, Dai-ichi Life and Nippon Life, and A+/Stable for Meiji Yasuda and Sumitomo Life.

The credit effect has been positive so far. Fitch says Japanese insurers target mid-sized US insurers with relatively low credit risk, avoid large natural catastrophe and commodity exposure, and favour specialty lines. Parental support has helped the subsidiaries: Fitch upgraded Resolution Life's US subsidiary, and Protective Life was upgraded two notches to AA-/Stable after Dai-ichi's acquisition. Nearly all Japanese-owned US subsidiaries have performed soundly with steady growth, according to the commentary.

Korea is following, from a smaller base. Korean insurers have historically concentrated on Southeast Asia, such as Vietnam and Indonesia, with minority or strategic stakes. Fitch says cross-border M&A reached about US$2.6 billion in 2025, over 75% of the total M&A value in the past five years. The most active groups are DB Insurance, Samsung Fire & Marine, Hanwha Life and Samsung Life. Hanwha Life acquired 75% of the US brokerage Velocity Clearing in 2025 and 40% of PT Bank Nationalnobu in Indonesia, and DB Insurance acquired Fortegra for US$1.65 billion, which Fitch describes as the first 100% acquisition of a US insurer by a Korean firm and the largest Korean cross-border insurance deal to date. Fitch sees these deals as credit-neutral to mildly positive in the short term, if capital management and integration are prudent.

There are risks. Concentration is the first. Fitch estimates that about 20% of major Japanese life insurers' profits come from North America, with a higher share for non-life insurers: about 60% of Tokio Marine's group income comes from the US, and about 30% of Sompo's, for the fiscal year to March 2025. That makes Japanese insurers more exposed to spillover from US real estate and private credit shocks. Fitch expects more issuance of subordinated bonds to fund acquisitions, particularly by Japanese insurers, since such debt counts as a regulatory capital buffer. In Korea, laws limit insurers' borrowing, so acquisitions are mostly funded from internal liquidity. Fitch estimates that DB Insurance's K-ICS ratio will fall by 15 to 20 percentage points after Fortegra, and that Hanwha Life's ratio fell about 2 points after Velocity. Macroeconomic conditions, geopolitics and regulation could strain buyers and their subsidiaries.

For sellers in the US and Europe, the message is that long-term buyers are available. For customers of acquired companies, the typical pattern is continuity, with the acquired brand and management kept in place. For regulators, the growth of cross-border ownership raises questions about group capital and supervision. This article reports Fitch's views and is not investment advice.

More than half of Fitch-rated Japanese insurers have done M&A in the past decade; major deals total about JPY 4.5 trillion (about US$35 billion), 86% of it in the US.
Japan's population has declined for 14 consecutive years and Korean insurance revenue growth is projected below 5% in 2026, pushing both sets of insurers abroad.

Korean cross-border M&A reached about US$2.6 billion in 2025, over 75% of total M&A value in five years; Fitch estimates DB Insurance's K-ICS ratio will fall 15-20% after buying Fortegra for US$1.65 billion.
Concentration is a risk: about 20% of major Japanese life insurers' profits come from North America, around 60% of Tokio Marine's group income comes from the US and about 30% of Sompo's.
why_it_matters: Japan and Korea have ageing populations and slow insurance growth at home. Their insurers' purchases abroad are reshaping the US and European specialty and life markets and could expose them to American credit and real estate shocks.

title: US Property Insurance Buyers Get Their Best Market in Years as Capacity Returns, Artex Says, but Casualty and Data Centre Values Remain Challenges
summary: Artex's Alternative View Spring 2026 says US commercial property buyers are eagerly using the most favourable market in several years to renegotiate terms and lower deductibles, while casualty remains pressured by social inflation.
description:
Buyers of US commercial property insurance have a stronger hand than they have had for years. That is the message of The Alternative View, a spring 2026 report from Artex Risk Solutions, the captive and alternative-risk specialist, as covered by Reinsurance News. According to the report, US property insureds are eagerly taking advantage of the most favourable market conditions they have experienced in several years. Capacity is plentiful, and carriers are keen to grow their property portfolios. As a result, many insureds are renegotiating terms that had become restrictive during the hard market and, in some cases, are securing lower deductibles. This article summarises the Reinsurance News coverage of the report. An earlier version of this article described the relief as applying broadly across US commercial insurance. The report is clear that casualty is a different story, and the article now reflects that.

Why did conditions improve? Artex points to a benign year for catastrophes. In 2025, no hurricane made landfall in the United States for the first time since 2015. That helped offset losses from the January 2025 California wildfires. After years of above-average rate increases, catastrophe-driven layered and shared property programmes are now seeing rate relief. Layered and shared programmes are structures in which several insurers each take a slice of a large property risk, and they are the part of the market where price falls usually show up first when capital returns. The result for buyers is not just lower rates. It is also the ability to negotiate on terms, such as deductibles and sublimits, that often matter more to a claim than the headline price.

Is this just a US trend? The same pattern is visible elsewhere. WTW's specialty survey, summarised in a separate article on this site, found that property and energy rates saw the steepest falls at the January 2026 renewals. Lockton, in its fiscal 2026 results, also noted that global property rates have softened as capacity and competition rose. The three sources use different data, so they should not be combined into a single figure, but they point in the same direction.

What does Artex say is still difficult? The first issue is valuation. The report flags accurate property valuations as a challenge, especially for data centres, which it describes as one of the fastest-growing commercial property segments. Artex says hyperscale facilities can carry insured values of $1 billion to $5 billion, and many sit in remote areas with severe convective storm or wildfire exposure. If a building and its equipment are insured for less than their replacement cost, the buyer may find that a claim is not fully paid. If insurers underestimate the values at risk, they may be undercharging for the exposure. Either way, both sides have a reason to take valuations seriously.

The second issue is casualty. Artex argues that rate increases alone will not restore the sector's health. It says litigation funding and social inflation are impairing most casualty lines, and that social inflation drives claim severity more than rising costs do. Social inflation refers to claims costs rising faster than general inflation, because of larger court awards, more litigation and changing attitudes to liability. Nuclear verdicts, defined in the report as jury awards above $10 million, are rising, prompting carriers to raise attachment points, add exclusions and struggle to price risk. Commercial auto has been hit hardest. Citing the American Transportation Research Institute, Artex says the median nuclear verdict reached $36 million by 2022, a 50% increase over 2013.

What should buyers do? The report does not give a checklist, but the logic of its findings suggests some practical steps. Buyers can ask their brokers to test the market on property programmes at renewal, to seek broader terms and lower deductibles rather than only lower premiums, and to review valuations so that limits are adequate. For casualty, buyers should expect that price and terms may not improve, and may want to consider alternative structures. Artex is a provider of captive and alternative-risk services, so its report naturally pays attention to such options, and readers should keep in mind that it has a commercial interest in the subject.

What does it mean for insurers? A softening property market is a natural result of strong profits and returning capital. The risk is that prices fall faster than the underlying exposure, especially if the benign catastrophe year is followed by a more active one. The Artex report does not forecast the 2026 hurricane season, and nothing in it should be read as a prediction.

For the wider economy, property insurance is a cost of owning and building almost anything. Lower prices can help borrowers and developers, and the data centre boom adds a new type of risk that the market is still learning to value. This article reports Artex's views and is not investment advice.

key_points: Artex says US property insureds are 'eagerly taking advantage' of the most favourable market conditions in several years, with ample capacity and carriers keen to grow property books.
Many insureds are renegotiating previously restrictive terms and, in some cases, securing lower deductibles; catastrophe-exposed layered and shared programmes are seeing rate relief.
2025 saw no US hurricane landfall for the first time since 2015, which helped offset losses from the January 2025 California wildfires.

Artex flags property valuation as a challenge, especially for data centres: hyperscale facilities can carry insured values of $1 billion to $5 billion, often in areas with severe convective storm or wildfire exposure.
On casualty, Artex says rate increases alone will not restore health; social inflation and litigation funding are impairing most lines, with commercial auto hit hardest.
why_it_matters: Property insurance costs feed into rents, construction budgets and company margins. A softer market lets buyers negotiate, but the uneven picture across property and casualty means that a lower property bill does not mean cheaper insurance across the board.
